question.text: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from a soccer game. During the game, he was about to kick the ball when another player collided with his leg from the front. He was unable to stand up after this collision and reported severe knee pain. On presentation, he was found to have a mild knee effusion. Physical exam showed that his knee could be pushed posteriorly at 90 degrees of flexion but it could not be pulled anteriorly in the same position. The anatomic structure that was most likely injured in this patient has which of the following characteristics?

options.A: Runs anteriorly from the medial femoral condyle
options.B: Runs medially from the lateral femoral condyle
options.C: Runs posteriorly from the lateral femoral condyle
options.D: Runs posteriorly from the medial femoral condyle
options.F: I don't know or cannot answer

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's inability to pull the knee anteriorly while pushing it posteriorly at 90 degrees of flexion strongly suggests a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury. The PCL runs posteriorly from the medial femoral condyle and prevents the tibia from sliding backward relative to the femur.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Inability to pull the knee anteriorly while pushing it posteriorly at 90 degrees of flexion.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury is a common knee injury, but the inability to pull the knee anteriorly makes PCL injury more likely. Meniscal tears can cause pain and swelling, but the specific mechanism of injury and the posterior pull test point more towards a ligamentous injury. A lateral collateral ligament (LCL) injury is less likely given the mechanism of injury and the posterior pull test result.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient's inability to extend the knee at 90 degrees while it can be flexed posteriorly suggests a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury. The PCL runs posteriorly from the medial femoral condyle to the tibial plateau, which matches the described location. The inability to extend the knee indicates PCL disruption, as it resists anterior translation of the tibia.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The inability to extend the knee at 90 degrees while it can be flexed posteriorly
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: MCL sprain, meniscus tear, and patellar dislocation were considered but ruled out by the specific directional preference of the injury (posterior direction) and the presence of knee effusion which is more consistent with ligament injury than meniscal or patellar issues.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The patient’s inability to extend the knee posteriorly at 90 degrees but inability to pull the tibia anteriorly (posterior drawer test positive) is classic for a posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) injury. The PCL originates from the posterior aspect of the medial femoral condyle and inserts on the posterior aspect of the tibia. This injury mechanism (posterior force to the tibia) and physical exam findings strongly point to PCL injury.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Posterior drawer test positive at 90 degrees of flexion, indicating PCL injury.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury was considered but ruled out because the ACL is tested with anterior drawer and Lachman tests, which were not described as positive. Meniscal tears or collateral ligament injuries were less likely given the specific posterior instability finding.

openbio_8b.clinical_reasoning: Based on the patient's inability to push the tibia anteriorly at 90 degrees of flexion, the most likely injured structure is the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). The ACL is a key ligament that prevents anterior translation of the tibia on the femur and is commonly injured in sports-related knee injuries.
openbio_8b.critical_evidence: Inability to push the tibia anteriorly at 90 degrees of flexion

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: A: Quadriceps tendon (would expect inability to extend the knee at any angle); B: Lateral collateral ligament (more related to instability than extension); C: Semitendinosus tendon (injury may affect flexion, not extension); E: None of the above (not supported by the key findings).
